exercise.name: Dumbbell Lying One Arm Pronated Triceps Extension

reference.title: Dumbbell Lying One Arm Pronated Triceps Extension
reference.listing: Page could not be read (gymvisual.com blocked by the proxy); movement taken from the exercise name and standard coaching practice
reference.note: Reference used only to identify the movement. No GymVisual media is stored here; this rig, model and animation are original.

breathing.pattern: Inhale as the dumbbell lowers beside the head, exhale as you straighten the arm.
breathing.cadence: About 2.2 s down, 0.3 s pause, 1.4 s up

prescription.load: Dumbbell load is user-chosen: pick a weight you can lift for the target reps with 1-3 reps in reserve (RIR 1-3, about RPE 7-9).
prescription.progression: More reps, then the next dumbbell.

cues.text: Lie on a flat bench, feet planted. Hold one dumbbell straight up over the shoulder, overhand grip (palm facing your feet, handle across the body); rest the other hand on your stomach.
Keep the upper arm still and breathe in as you bend the elbow, lowering the dumbbell back toward the top of the head on the same side.
Dumbbell just above and beside the forehead, palm facing the ceiling, elbow pointing up; feel the stretch in the back of the arm.
Breathe out and straighten the elbow along the same path.
Arm straight, squeeze the triceps, repeat; then switch arms.

mistakes.mistake: Upper arm drifting toward the feet as you press
mistakes.fix: Keep the elbow pointing at the same spot on the ceiling; only the forearm moves.
Keep both shoulder blades on the bench; brace lightly.

mistakes.mistake: Inner plate drifting into the forehead
mistakes.fix: Lower the dumbbell to just above the head and stop there; use a short-handled dumbbell.
Straighten the elbow without snapping it.

kinematics.norm: From straight to about 90-100 degrees, stopping before the dumbbell reaches the head (clinical opinion)
Vertical over the shoulder and still (clinical opinion)
Pronated (overhand): palm toward the feet with the arm straight, toward the ceiling at the bottom; the handle stays across the body (clinical opinion)
The forearm swings back in the plane of the arm, so the dumbbell ends just above the head on the working side; stop short of touching it (clinical opinion)
Rests on the stomach; some lifters steady the working upper arm with it instead (clinical opinion)
Feet flat on the floor with the knees bent about 90 degrees, like the bench set-up in Solstad 2020 (head, shoulders and hips on the bench)
Controlled, about 2 s down and 1-1.5 s up (clinical opinion)

cautions: Lower toward the top of the head, not onto the face; the inner plate passes close to the forehead, so control the bottom and use a fixed-plate dumbbell.
Elbow pain: shorten the range and use a lighter dumbbell (clinical opinion).
Keep the wrist straight over the forearm; a bent-back wrist under the dumbbell strains it.
Stop if sharp pain, numbness or tingling occurs.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
modify: Shoulder discomfort: let the upper arm tilt slightly toward the head.
Elbow discomfort: lighter dumbbell, shorter range.
regressions: Two-arm lying extension with light dumbbells.

muscleNotes.triceps_r: Only mover: straightens the elbow while the upper arm stays vertical. Long and lateral head activity differed in lying barbell triceps extensions (Boehler 2011); the long head works at a longer length the higher the arm is raised (Maeo and Kanehisa). The overhand grip keeps the forearm pronated, which some lifters find easier on the elbow than a neutral grip (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.forearm_flexors_r: Grip the handle and hold the wrist straight.
muscleNotes.post_deltoid_r: Holds the upper arm vertical as the dumbbell lowers behind the elbow.
muscleNotes.core: Keeps the trunk still on the bench.

guides.label: Forearm swings back, upper arm still
Elbow a little past 90 at the bottom
